body.text: Senator Leah Blyth, who is understood to have had a falling out with SA Liberal president Alex Antic, says she has lost confidence in the party's ability to "save this country".

Murray Watt says Liberal Party is in 'complete disarray'
Environment Minister Murray Watt has stepped up to take a whack at the Coalition over Senator Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation.
The environment minister says the Liberal Party is in "complete disarray" and that One Nation is "stealing" Coalition MPs.
Speaking to reporters in the press gallery, Watt says he thinks it shows the Liberal Party isn't capable of running the country.
"This is obviously a terrible day for Angus Taylor and the Liberal Party. He's showing that he can't govern his party, therefore he simply cannot govern the country," Watt says.
"What we're seeing from One Nation over a long period of time is that they've been stealing Liberal Party policies and now they're stealing Liberal Party politicians."
Thompson says Blyth wants to 'save her own job', labels her disloyal
Liberal MP Phil Thompson says he thinks Leah Blyth wants to save her own job and has shown disloyalty to the Liberals by defecting to One Nation.
Upon her defection, the SA senator said Australians can no longer trust the Liberals, and that One Nation is the only party that can "turn this country around".
Blyth, who was the shadow assistant minister for defence infrastructure, was understood to have not been likely to secure a winnable Senate spot at the next federal election.
This morning, One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson says Blyth approached her to defect to the party.
Speaking to News24, Thompson says he found out about the defection in the newspaper this morning "like everyone else".

"I think we should just call it for what it is. Leah Blyth had lost her numbers in the pre-selection, wasn't going to be preselected for the Liberal Party in South Australia and is more focussed on income rather than outcome," Thompson says.

"I think she showed disloyalty. She hasn't, she's never once mentioned this in any of the shadow ministry meetings that I've been a part of or raised any concerns."We've just got a call for what it is, mate. She's not a One Nation person. She never has been. She just wants to save her own job."
"I think she showed disloyalty. She hasn't, she's never once mentioned this in any of the shadow ministry meetings that I've been a part of or raised any concerns.
"We've just got a call for what it is, mate. She's not a One Nation person. She never has been. She just wants to save her own job."
Hanson and Blyth to hold joint press conference this morning
We've just had word that One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson and SA senator Leah Blyth will hold a joint press conference this morning.
The senators will be stepping up at 10:10am AEDT here at Parliament House in Canberra. For folks joining along in SA, that's 9:40am for you.
It will be the first time the South Australian senator has faced the media following her defection to the right-wing party.
We'll bring you that press conference here live (as always!) as soon as it happens!
Shoebridge says Greens wanted Labor to go further on trusts
Greens Leader David Shoebridge says his party would have liked Labor's discretionary trusts changes to have been tougher.
The government's move to place a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts passed the Senate last night after Labor and the Greens reached a deal.
In exchange for the Greens' support, Labor agreed to "eliminate" the difference between the fuel excise paid by people who own private jets and the fuel excise paid by motorists.
But speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Shoebridge says he would have liked to have seen an exclusion for any of the funds coming from discretionary trusts going to charities.

"We couldn't get Labor to agree to crack down on money going to cults and private schools. I think that says a lot about Labor, but we did get that additional funding to have more integrity in the system," Shoebridge says."We got a clear statement that discretionary trusts can't be funnelled through to school fees, and there'll be actual some additional regulatory powers looking at that."

"We couldn't get Labor to agree to crack down on money going to cults and private schools. I think that says a lot about Labor, but we did get that additional funding to have more integrity in the system," Shoebridge says.
"We got a clear statement that discretionary trusts can't be funnelled through to school fees, and there'll be actual some additional regulatory powers looking at that."
Conroy says spike in oil prices led to uptick in inflation rate
Changing tack for just a moment, and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy says yesterday's inflation figures were disappointing but not unexpected.
Inflation rose half a per cent in October, in original terms, to 4.9 per cent, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data.
Conroy says a global spike in oil prices due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz were a factor and flowed through to the domestic economy.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Conroy says the upcoming mid-year fiscal and economy outlook will provide net savings.

"We're clear that people are doing it tough. This global inflation spike is hitting everyone around the world, and that's why we're very strong on the Strait of Hormuz needs to be reopened and oil needs to flow," Conroy says.
Asked if he will have to find net savings in his portfolio, Conroy says he won't get ahead of the budget process.
One Nation's prospects in Victoria state election 'going to be tough', Joyce says
Barnaby Joyce says One Nation's prospects in Victoria at this weekend's state election are "going to be tough".
The NSW One Nation MP says Labor preferences may decide whether the right-wing party can win seats in Victoria's lower house.
Joyce says that will depend how the primary vote falls in each electorate. He says the Liberals will likely benefit from Labor preferences.

"It's going to be tough because the socialists have done such an atrocious that the Labor socialists will come in many instances third, probably many instances fourth," Joyce says."Really the only sort of issue about people who vote for them is about where their preferences go."
"It's going to be tough because the socialists have done such an atrocious that the Labor socialists will come in many instances third, probably many instances fourth," Joyce says.
"Really the only sort of issue about people who vote for them is about where their preferences go."
Joyce says One Nation is not focused on seeking out MPs from other parties
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says his party is not focused on seeking out parliamentarians to join the right-wing party's team.
Earlier, Nationals senator Matt Canavan suggested he had to convince some Coalition members not to defect to One Nation.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Joyce says he thinks it's a "fair appraisal" by Canavan.
"We don't really focus on that. We don't really even focus on going out and finding other people to join One Nation, we focus on what our job is," Joyce says.
"If people make moves towards joining One Nation then that's definitely in the realm of Pauline [Hanson] as to her assessment of whether they are appropriate."
Key Event
Joyce says Hanson kept Blyth defection 'very close to her chest'
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says Pauline Hanson kept Leah Blyth's defection to her party "very close to her chest".
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Joyce says the rest of the party's parliamentary team became aware of the defection "much later on".
"Pauline and Leah had a yarn about it for a period of time that we weren't aware of it. But I'm very, very, very enthusiastic and welcoming about it," Joyce says.
Asked if Blyth defected to One Nation because she would be relegated to an unwinnable Senate spot at the next election, Joyce says that's a "hypothetical question".

"I don't believe that people join One Nation for that reason. The join One Nation because they have conservative view of the world and they want to be a part of what is genuinely a conservative party."
Key Event
Hanson says Blyth approached her, felt 'frustrated' with the Liberal Party
One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson has just dropped into 2GB here at parliament to talk about the defection of SA senator Leah Blyth.
Blyth, who was the shadow assistant minister for defence infrastructure, announced her defection to One Nation overnight.
The One Nation leader says Blyth approached her to defect to the party. She says the SA senator felt "frustrated".
"She's frustrated because she said she cannot see the Libs under Angus Taylor turning around the economy," Hanson said of Blyth.

"She said [to Hanson] the infighting that goes on constantly all the time, she's had a gutful of it. She said: 'I don't leave my husband and three children to come to this place and feel that I'm wasting my time being away from them,' she said."
Hanson hasn't ruled out further sandwich press steaks and defections to her party.
McKenzie says Blyth's defection is 'self-interested'
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie says she's disappointed about Leah Blyth's defection from the Liberals to One Nation.
Speaking to Channel Nine, McKenzie says people "deciding to defect for their own personal political reasons" is "self-interested".

"There are some serious challenges out there and the Liberal and the National party at a federal level are focused on solving those problem," McKenzie says."We're not going to be distracted by that over some steaks."
"There are some serious challenges out there and the Liberal and the National party at a federal level are focused on solving those problem," McKenzie says.
"We're not going to be distracted by that over some steaks."
Blythe is understood to have had a falling-out with conservative powerbroker and SA Liberal Party president Alex Antic.
It was understood she was unlikely to have secured a winnable Senate spot at the next federal election.
Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy says she's not surprised to see the defection of the former SA Liberal party president.
Key Event
Canavan says Blyth's defection to One Nation 'smacks of self-interest'
We're getting the first political reaction to SA senator Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation in the last few hours.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says people who voted for Blyth as a Liberal in South Australia have a right to feel let-down.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Canavan says One Nation is turning into "turncoat town" and picking members from other parties.
He says he didn't have much warning on Blyth's defection.

"It's right that people feel a bit let-down when someone's elected by them ticking a party box, changes parties after the election. So that's very disappointing and that's… but it's a pattern of behaviour from One Nation. They are turning into turncoat town here, right?" Canavan says.
"It smacks of self-interest to me. Good luck to her. I suppose you always back that horse, as Paul Keating said."
Asked if he's talked anyone out of defecting, Canavan says: "I don't know. I don't know if you'd say it like that".
Key Event
Hanson forward sizzled Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation last night
Ahead of SA senator Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation, the party's leader Pauline Hanson quite literally forward sizzled the announcement.
In a video posted to social media at 8:20pm Canberra time last night from her Parliament House office kitchen, Hanson teased the announcement.
"Close the lid, alright. Cooks it both sides. Guess who this is for? Keep guessing," Hanson said in a video posted to X (formerly Twitter).
It's a trope Hanson used to foreshadow Barnaby Joyce's defection from the Nationals to One Nation about a year ago when she cooked a steak on a toaster for the New England MP.
Key Event
Hanson says Blyth's defection will 'resonate' with Liberal voters
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says her party is "delighted" to welcome SA senator Leah Blyth to its ranks.
The Queensland senator says she thinks Blyth's decision to defect to One Nation from the Liberals will "resonate" with Australians who have supported the Liberals.
"Senator Blyth's decision will resonate with Australians who have supported the Liberals for years and feel the party has abandoned them," Hanson said in a statement with Blyth.

"Australians want immigration brought under control, affordable energy and a government that stops wasting their money. The growing One Nation team will offer Australians exactly that."Senator Blyth will be One Nation's first South Australian senator and will build on One Nation's expanding support within the state."
"Australians want immigration brought under control, affordable energy and a government that stops wasting their money. The growing One Nation team will offer Australians exactly that.
"Senator Blyth will be One Nation's first South Australian senator and will build on One Nation's expanding support within the state."

Blyth says she's left the Liberals because Australians can't trust the party
OK so let's get a little more on the news South Australian senator Leah Blyth has defected to One Nation.
In a joint statement with One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson, Blyth says she's left the Liberals because of growing government spending, "excessive" immigration and net zero policies.
She says Australians can no longer trust the Liberals, and that One Nation is the only party that can "turn the country around".
"Australia is a country worth fighting for. I want our children to grow up proud of their country, with the freedom and opportunity to build a better life," Blyth says.

"I am joining Pauline Hanson and the One Nation team to fight for that future."One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around."
"I am joining Pauline Hanson and the One Nation team to fight for that future.
"One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around."
Blythe, who entered parliament in February last year, was understood to likely secure an unwinnable Senate spot at the next election after a falling-out with SA Liberal president Alex Antic.
Key Event
SA Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation
South Australian Liberal senator Leah Blyth has defected to One Nation, in a major blow to Angus Taylor's Coalition.
Blyth, a member of Taylor's shadow ministry and former president of the SA Liberal Party, will become Pauline Hanson's first South Australian senator.

She says she believes the Albanese government is damaging the country but has lost confidence in the opposition's ability to address issues including immigration, government spending and energy policy.
"But I can no longer in good conscience tell Australians that the Liberal Party can save this country," she says.
Blyth entered parliament in February last year, filling the vacancy left by Simon Birmingham.
It is understood she was unlikely to secure a winnable spot on the Liberals' Senate ticket at the next federal election, following a falling-out with conservative factional powerbroker Alex Antic.
Her recruitment comes almost a year after former Nationals leader Barnaby Joyce defected to One Nation.
Hanson even cooked Blyth a steak using a sandwich press, as she did for Joyce before he joined the party.
